g1.text: Together with other monks, Govinda used to spend the time of rest between pilgrimages in the pleasure-grove, which the courtesan Kamala had given to the followers of Gotama for a gift. He heard talk of an old ferryman, who lived one day's journey away by the river, and who was regarded as a wise man by many. When Govinda went back on his way, he chose the path to the ferry, eager to see the ferryman. Because, though he had lived his entire life by the rules, though he was also looked upon with veneration by the younger monks on account of his age and his modesty, the restlessness and the searching still had not perished from his heart.

g2.text: When someone is searching," said Siddhartha, "then it might easily happen that the only thing his eyes still see is that what he searches for, that he is unable to find anything, to let anything enter his mind, because he always thinks of nothing but the object of his search, because he has a goal, because he is obsessed by the goal. Searching means: having a goal. But finding means: being free, being open, having no goal. You, O venerable one, are perhaps indeed a searcher, because, striving for your goal, there are many things you don't see, which are directly in front of your eyes.

g3.text: A long time ago, O venerable one, many years ago, you've once before been at this river and have found a sleeping man by the river, and have sat down with him to guard his sleep. But, O Govinda, you did not recognise the sleeping man." Astonished, as if he had been the object of a magic spell, the monk looked into the ferryman's eyes. "Are you Siddhartha?" he asked with a timid voice. "I wouldn't have recognised you this time as well! From my heart, I'm greeting you, Siddhartha; from my heart, I'm happy to see you once again! You've changed a lot, my friend.—And so you've now become a ferryman?

g4.text: Nevertheless, I have had many teachers since then. A beautiful courtesan has been my teacher for a long time, and a rich merchant was my teacher, and some gamblers with dice. Once, even a follower of Buddha, travelling on foot, has been my teacher; he sat with me when I had fallen asleep in the forest, on the pilgrimage. I've also learned from him, I'm also grateful to him, very grateful. But most of all, I have learned here from this river and from my predecessor, the ferryman Vasudeva. He was a very simple person, Vasudeva, he was no thinker, but he knew what is necessary just as well as Gotama, he was a perfect man, a saint.

g5.text: I've had thoughts, yes, and insight, again and again. Sometimes, for an hour or for an entire day, I have felt knowledge in me, as one would feel life in one's heart. There have been many thoughts, but it would be hard for me to convey them to you. Look, my dear Govinda, this is one of my thoughts, which I have found: wisdom cannot be passed on. Wisdom which a wise man tries to pass on to someone always sounds like foolishness.

g6.text: I have found a thought, Govinda, which you'll again regard as a joke or foolishness, but which is my best thought. It says: The opposite of every truth is just as true! That's like this: any truth can only be expressed and put into words when it is one-sided. Everything is one-sided which can be thought with thoughts and said with words, it's all one-sided, all just one half, all lacks completeness, roundness, oneness. When the exalted Gotama spoke in his teachings of the world, he had to divide it into Sansara and Nirvana, into deception and truth, into suffering and salvation.

g7.text: Here on this ferryboat, for instance, a man has been my predecessor and teacher, a holy man, who has for many years simply believed in the river, nothing else. He had noticed that the river's spoke to him, he learned from it, it educated and taught him, the river seemed to be a god to him, for many years he did not know that every wind, every cloud, every bird, every beetle was just as divine and knows just as much and can teach just as much as the worshipped river. But when this holy man went into the forests, he knew everything, knew more than you and me, without teachers, without books, only because he had believed in the river.

g8.text: Let the things be illusions or not, after all I would then also be an illusion, and thus they are always like me. This is what makes them so dear and worthy of veneration for me: they are like me. Therefore, I can love them. And this is now a teaching you will laugh about: love, O Govinda, seems to me to be the most important thing of all. To thoroughly understand the world, to explain it, to despise it, may be the thing great thinkers do. But I'm only interested in being able to love the world, not to despise it, not to hate it and me, to be able to look upon it and me and all beings with love and admiration and great respect.

g9.text: How should he not know love, he, who has discovered all elements of human existence in their transitoriness, in their meaninglessness, and yet loved people thus much, to use a long, laborious life only to help them, to teach them! Even with him, even with your great teacher, I prefer the thing over the words, place more importance on his acts and life than on his speeches, more on the gestures of his hand than his opinions. Not in his speech, not in his thoughts, I see his greatness, only in his actions, in his life.

g10.text: This Siddhartha is a bizarre person, he expresses bizarre thoughts, his teachings sound foolish. So differently sound the exalted one's pure teachings, clearer, purer, more comprehensible, nothing strange, foolish, or silly is contained in them. But different from his thoughts seemed to me Siddhartha's hands and feet, his eyes, his forehead, his breath, his smile, his greeting, his walk. Never again, after our exalted Gotama has become one with the Nirvana, never since then have I met a person of whom I felt: this is a holy man!

g11.text: As Govinda thought like this, and there was a conflict in his heart, he once again bowed to Siddhartha, drawn by love. Deeply he bowed to him who was calmly sitting. "Siddhartha," he spoke, "we have become old men. It is unlikely for one of us to see the other again in this incarnation. I see, beloved, that you have found peace. I confess that I haven't found it. Tell me, O honourable one, one more word, give me something on my way which I can grasp, which I can understand! Give me something to be with me on my path. It is often hard, my path, often dark, Siddhartha." Siddhartha said nothing and looked at him with the ever unchanged, quiet smile. Govinda stared at his face, with fear, with yearning, suffering, and the eternal search was visible in his look, eternal not-finding.

g12.text: Not knowing any more whether time existed, whether the vision had lasted a second or a hundred years, not knowing any more whether there existed a Siddhartha, a Gotama, a me and a you, feeling in his innermost self as if he had been wounded by a divine arrow, the injury of which tasted sweet, being enchanted and dissolved in his innermost self, Govinda still stood for a little while bent over Siddhartha's quiet face, which he had just kissed, which had just been the scene of all manifestations, all transformations, all existence. The face was unchanged, after under its surface the depth of the thousandfoldness had closed up again, he smiled silently, smiled quietly and softly, perhaps very benevolently, perhaps very mockingly, precisely as he used to smile, the exalted one.

g13.text: Deeply, Govinda bowed; tears he knew nothing of ran down his old face; like a fire burnt the feeling of the most intimate love, the humblest veneration in his heart. Deeply, he bowed, touching the ground, before him who was sitting motionlessly, whose smile reminded him of everything he had ever loved in his life, what had ever been valuable and holy to him in his life.

g15.text: The world, my friend Govinda, is not imperfect, or on a slow path towards perfection: no, it is perfect in every moment, all sin already carries the divine forgiveness in itself, all small children already have the old person in themselves, all infants already have death, all dying people the eternal life. It is not possible for any person to see how far another one has already progressed on his path; in the robber and dice-gambler, the Buddha is waiting; in the Brahmin, the robber is waiting.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Govinda wants to give up his robe and become a ferryman.
Govinda has found perfect peace and now wants to teach the ferryman the rules of Gotama.
Though old and respected, Govinda is still restless and goes to see the wise ferryman.
Govinda is looking for Kamala and her grove.
A.explanation: Govinda "chose the path to the ferry, eager to see the ferryman," because "the restlessness and the searching still had not perished from his heart." He has not found peace. Kamala's grove is only where the monks rest. He wants to see the ferryman, not become one.

A.prompt: According to Siddhartha, what did Govinda do at this river long ago?
options: He met Kamala in her grove.
He sat by a sleeping man to guard his sleep.
He bathed in the river.
He ferried a group of monks across the river.
A.explanation: Siddhartha says Govinda "found a sleeping man by the river, and... sat down with him to guard his sleep." He did not ferry anyone. Kamala is not mentioned here. Bathing is not mentioned. Govinda had once guarded Siddhartha's sleep by this river without knowing him.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "modesty" most nearly means
options: humility
shyness
wealth
strictness
A.explanation: The younger monks honour him "on account of his age and his modesty," a quality of humility. Shyness is a different sense; nothing says he avoids speaking. A monk has no wealth. Strictness is not suggested. The word names the humble quality that the younger monks honour in Govinda.

options: wants to stay at the river for good
is certain that his own path is the right one
has not found peace and longs for help
is angry at Siddhartha
A.explanation: He says, "I confess that I haven't found it... Give me something to be with me on my path," and "eternal not-finding" shows in his look. He is not certain. He bows "drawn by love," not angry. He speaks of parting, not staying.

A.prompt: What does Siddhartha say about wisdom?
options: It is the same thing as knowledge.
It can be learned quickly from a good teacher.
It cannot be passed on in words.
It belongs only to Gotama.
A.explanation: He says "wisdom cannot be passed on" and that taught wisdom "always sounds like foolishness." So it cannot be quickly learned from a teacher. He separates it from knowledge. Nothing limits it to Gotama. Siddhartha says wisdom can be lived and found, but not taught in words.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "Wisdom which a wise man tries to pass on to someone always sounds like foolishness."
"There have been many thoughts, but it would be hard for me to convey them to you."
"Sometimes, for an hour or for an entire day, I have felt knowledge in me"
"I've had thoughts, yes, and insight, again and again."
A.explanation: Only the line about wisdom that "always sounds like foolishness" states his claim about wisdom. "Felt knowledge in me" describes his experience. "Hard for me to convey them" is about his thoughts in general. "I've had thoughts" simply opens his answer.

A.prompt: The list of a courtesan, a merchant, gamblers and a monk mainly serves to
options: name his enemies in the city
show that Siddhartha has learned from many kinds of people
describe the city and its people
show that Siddhartha thinks all of these people were foolish
A.explanation: He says, "I have had many teachers since then," and names a courtesan, a merchant, gamblers and a monk. He is grateful, so he does not call them useless. They are teachers, not enemies. The city is not described. The list shows that Siddhartha learned from all kinds of people, not only from teachers.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha bows low to Govinda.
Govinda falls asleep in the hut.
Govinda leaves angrily, sure that Siddhartha's words were foolish.
Govinda bows in tears, full of love and reverence for Siddhartha.
A.explanation: Govinda bowed "touching the ground," with tears and "the most intimate love, the humblest veneration." He does not leave angrily. Siddhartha sits "motionlessly"; Govinda bows. No sleep is mentioned. The passage shows Govinda overwhelmed by love and reverence at the end.

A.prompt: According to the passage, what did the holy man believe in?
options: The stars and the moon
The river
The teachings of the Buddha
Books
A.explanation: He "for many years simply believed in the river, nothing else." Buddha's teachings are not named as his belief. Stars are not mentioned. He learned "without teachers, without books." The holy man learned everything simply by believing in the river.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "enchanted" most nearly means
options: cursed
tricked
bored
spellbound
A.explanation: Govinda is "enchanted and dissolved in his innermost self," held as if by a spell. The feeling is sweet, so "cursed" is wrong. "Bored" is the opposite. "Tricked" adds deceit that the passage does not suggest. The word describes Govinda being held as if by a spell after his vision.

options: finds Siddhartha's words strange but sees holiness in him
is jealous of Siddhartha's peace
thinks Siddhartha is foolish in speech and unholy in life
fully understands Siddhartha
A.explanation: He thinks "his teachings sound foolish," yet Siddhartha's "hands and feet, his eyes" seemed different: "this is a holy man!" He does not call him unholy. He does not fully understand. Jealousy is not shown. Govinda calls the words foolish but sees holiness in the whole man.

A.prompt: The words "like a fire burnt the feeling" suggest that Govinda's love is
options: fading
dangerous and harmful
pretended
intense and overwhelming
A.explanation: Love that burns "like a fire" is strong and overwhelming, as his tears and deep bow show. "Dangerous" takes the fire image too literally. It grows, not fades. His tears show it is real, not pretended. The fire image shows the strength of the love burning in Govinda's heart.

B.prompt: According to Siddhartha, what does finding mean?
options: Following one goal so closely that nothing distracts
Being free, being open, having no goal
Reaching the end of a road
Owning many things
B.explanation: "Finding means: being free, being open, having no goal." Following one goal is what searching means. Reaching a road's end and owning things are not mentioned. Siddhartha defines finding as freedom and openness, the opposite of searching. Reaching a road's end or owning things has nothing to do with it.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "progressed" most nearly means
options: advanced
rested
gone backward
spoken
B.explanation: No one can see "how far another one has already progressed on his path," so it means advanced. Going backward is the opposite. "Spoken" and "rested" do not fit movement along a path. The word describes how far a person has advanced on his path.

options: recognised Siddhartha at once in the ferryboat
is angry at being tricked
has never met Siddhartha before
has failed twice to recognise Siddhartha
B.explanation: Govinda says, "I wouldn't have recognised you this time as well!" after once failing to know the sleeping man. He did not recognise him at once. He is "happy to see you," not angry. They were friends from youth. Govinda fails twice to know his friend, once asleep and once as a ferryman.

options: His teacher told him to.
They are useful to him.
They are like him.
He has proved that they are real.
B.explanation: He says "they are like me. Therefore, I can love them." He does not prove they are real: "Let the things be illusions or not." No teacher's command is given. Usefulness is not his reason. Siddhartha loves things because they share his nature, whether real or illusion.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "To thoroughly understand the world, to explain it, to despise it, may be the thing great thinkers do."
"Let the things be illusions or not, after all I would then also be an illusion"
"This is what makes them so dear and worthy of veneration for me: they are like me."
"love, O Govinda, seems to me to be the most important thing of all"
B.explanation: Only "they are like me" gives his reason. The illusion line sets the question aside. The great thinkers line describes what others do. "Love... the most important thing" states a value, not why things are dear to him. The chosen line gives the reason directly: "they are like me."

B.prompt: The phrase "perhaps very benevolently, perhaps very mockingly" mainly serves to
options: show anger at Govinda
show that the smile cannot be fully read
show that Siddhartha is openly laughing at his friend
describe Gotama's robe
B.explanation: The paired "perhaps" phrases leave the smile uncertain, kind or mocking, "precisely as... the exalted one." He smiles "silently," not openly laughing. No robe is described. Anger is not suggested. The phrase leaves it open whether the smile is kind or mocking.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Gotama's teachings are false and should be forgotten by his followers.
Knowledge cannot be taught to anyone.
Time is the only real thing in the world.
Words make every truth one-sided, while the world itself is not.
B.explanation: Truth put into words "is one-sided... all lacks completeness, roundness, oneness." He says Gotama "had to divide" the world; the teachings are not called false. The passage does not discuss time. Teaching knowledge is not his subject; his point is about words and truth. Siddhartha argues that words split the world in two, though the world itself is whole.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "laborious" most nearly means
options: short
full of hard work
joyful
lazy, idle and slow
B.explanation: Gotama used "a long, laborious life only to help them, to teach them," so it means full of hard work. Lazy is the opposite. It is called "long," not short. "Joyful" misses the effort. The word describes Gotama's long life of hard work spent helping and teaching others.

B.prompt: The contrast "Searching means... But finding means" mainly serves to
options: set searching against finding to show why Govinda misses things
praise Govinda for his long search
show that searching and finding are really the same thing
describe the river and its voice
B.explanation: Searching is "having a goal"; finding is "having no goal," explaining why Govinda misses what is "in front of your eyes." They are opposed, not the same. The point is a gentle criticism, not praise. The river is not described.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha believes
options: books are the best teachers of all
Vasudeva was foolish
only a river can teach anything worth knowing
anything in nature can teach as much as the river
B.explanation: Every wind, cloud, bird and beetle "can teach just as much as the worshipped river." So the river is not the only teacher. The holy man learned "without books." Vasudeva is called "a holy man." Siddhartha says every wind, cloud, bird and beetle can teach as much as the river.

B.prompt: Govinda's private first-person thoughts mainly reveal
options: his mixed judgment of Siddhartha's words and person
his wish to leave the order
his hatred of Gotama
that he plans to report Siddhartha to the monks
B.explanation: His thoughts call the teachings "foolish" yet the man "holy," a mixed judgment. No plan to report him appears. He reveres "our exalted Gotama." Leaving the order is not suggested. His private thoughts show him torn between the words he dislikes and the man he loves.

B.prompt: How does Passage 2 relate to Govinda's state in Passage 1?
options: It shows him giving up his search and going back home at last.
It shows him becoming a ferryman himself.
It shows his restless, searching heart deeply moved at last.
It shows him trying to teach Siddhartha.
B.explanation: Passage 1 says "the restlessness and the searching still had not perished"; Passage 2 shows him in tears with "the most intimate love." He does not go to his father's house. He bows rather than teaches. He does not become a ferryman.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: The world is perfect in every moment, with the future already present in everyone.
Robbers can never change their nature, however long they live.
Small children are wiser than the old.
The world slowly improves, and only the very best people will one day become a Buddha.
C.explanation: The world "is perfect in every moment," and the future Buddha is already within the sinner. He rejects a "slow path towards perfection." The Buddha waits even "in the robber." Children have "the old person in themselves," not more wisdom.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha values
options: despising himself and the world
only beautiful things
loving the world above explaining it
explaining the world above loving it
C.explanation: Explaining the world "may be the thing great thinkers do. But I'm only interested in being able to love the world." Explaining is not ranked higher. He refuses "to hate it and me." He loves "all beings," not only beautiful things.

C.prompt: The pairs "Sansara and Nirvana... deception and truth... suffering and salvation" mainly serve to
options: name Gotama's best students
show how teaching must divide the world in two
describe the river
list the places Gotama visited on his long walks
C.explanation: Gotama "had to divide it into Sansara and Nirvana, into deception and truth, into suffering and salvation"; teaching requires division. They are concepts, not places or students. The river is not mentioned. The pairs show how teaching must split the world into opposites.

C.prompt: How does Siddhartha judge Gotama's greatness?
options: By the clever arguments in his many speeches
By his many students
By his wealth
By his acts and life rather than his words
C.explanation: "Not in his speech, not in his thoughts, I see his greatness, only in his actions, in his life." So clever speech is wrong. Wealth is not mentioned. Students appear only as people he helped, not as the measure. Siddhartha sees Gotama's greatness in his deeds rather than his words.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "to use a long, laborious life only to help them, to teach them!"
"Even with him, even with your great teacher, I prefer the thing over the words"
"How should he not know love, he, who has discovered all elements of human existence"
"Not in his speech, not in his thoughts, I see his greatness, only in his actions, in his life."
C.explanation: Only "Not in his speech... only in his actions" states how he judges greatness. "How should he not know love" argues Gotama knew love. "To help them, to teach them" describes Gotama's work. "I prefer the thing" is general, not his measure of greatness.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "yearning" most nearly means
options: longing
pride
hatred
sleepiness
C.explanation: "With fear, with yearning, suffering" in a look of "eternal not-finding" shows longing. Hatred does not fit his love. Sleepiness and pride do not fit someone begging for help. The word describes the longing visible in Govinda's face as he begs for help.

C.prompt: The image of being "wounded by a divine arrow, the injury of which tasted sweet" suggests that Govinda's experience is
options: boring
a real injury caused in anger
painful yet joyful and sacred
frightening only
C.explanation: The arrow is "divine" and the injury "tasted sweet," so the moment is painful yet joyful and holy. It is a figure, not a real wound, and there is no anger. It is not boring. "Sweet" shows it is not only frightening.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha hesitates to share his thoughts because
options: wisdom loses its truth when put into words
Govinda has insulted him and does not deserve it
he is tired
he has none
C.explanation: He says "it would be hard for me to convey them," since wisdom put into words "always sounds like foolishness." Govinda has not insulted him. He has "had thoughts... again and again." Tiredness is not mentioned. He fears that wisdom spoken aloud will only sound like foolishness.

C.prompt: The reversal "in the robber and dice-gambler, the Buddha is waiting; in the Brahmin, the robber is waiting" mainly serves to
options: describe a crime
praise gamblers
show that Brahmins are worse than robbers and gamblers
show that holiness and sin exist in everyone
C.explanation: The mirrored clauses show both possibilities "waiting" in every person. They do not rank Brahmins below robbers. Gamblers are not praised. No crime is described. The mirrored clauses show both good and evil waiting in every single person, whatever his rank or past.

C.prompt: Siddhartha's repeated address "O venerable one" mainly reflects
options: his wish to be paid for the crossing
the respectful distance he keeps while Govinda does not recognise him
his anger at the monk for asking so many foolish and tiresome questions
his fear of monks
C.explanation: He speaks to Govinda formally, "O venerable one," while still unrecognised, before he names him. No anger is shown. Fear does not fit his calm smile. Payment is not mentioned. The formal address keeps a respectful distance while Govinda does not yet recognise his friend.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 relate to the idea in Passage 1?
options: It shows that the river is a danger to travellers.
It gives an example of someone who found wisdom without chasing teachings.
It describes Govinda's own teacher and master.
It shows that searching hard for a goal is the only way to wisdom.
C.explanation: Passage 1 says finding means "having no goal"; in Passage 2 the holy man knew everything "without teachers, without books," simply believing in the river. Passage 2 does not praise hard searching. The holy man is Siddhartha's teacher, not Govinda's. The river is not dangerous.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 answer Govinda's view in Passage 1?
options: It shows that Siddhartha's teachings were foolish after all.
It shows Govinda leaving at once.
His vision shows the holiness he sensed in Siddhartha.
It shows Siddhartha in anger.
C.explanation: In Passage 1 he senses "this is a holy man!"; in Passage 2 Siddhartha smiles "precisely as he used to smile, the exalted one." Passage 2 does not call the teachings foolish. Govinda stays "bent over." Siddhartha smiles "quietly and softly," not in anger.
